newsitem.title: JAPAN: Bandai sinks, Sega rises after merger call-off.
newsitem.headline: Bandai sinks, Sega rises after merger call-off.

text.p: Shares in toymaker Bandai Co Ltd sagged and those of Sega Enterprises Ltd firmed on Wednesday in reaction to the sudden cancellation of a merger which would have formed Japan's largest game company.
There was some discouragement stemming from a lost business opportunity, but brokers said worries over the future management of Bandai were also bruising the share price.

"It seems that the Bandai president was unable to persuade the firm's managers into accepting the merger," a broker at a "Big Four" brokerage said. "Investors fear the absence of unity within the firm may hinder growth."
At the end of the Wednesday session, Bandai had shed 90 yen to 2,670 while Sega was marginally firmer by 80 yen at 3,780.

Bandai known for its Power Rangers and virtual pet toy "Tamagotchi" and Sega, maker of the Sega Saturn 32-bit video-game player said in January they would merge to create a global entertainment giant likened to Walt Disney Co.
But the merger had been haunted from the start by speculation that the it could be delayed by opposition from mid-level managers at Bandai, a closely knit firm.

"There had been much bright news stemming from Tamagotchi, but the cancellation revealed the conservative stance of the firm's management which may even lead to debate over leadership within the firm," a dealer at a "Big Four" brokerage said.
Bandai said on Wednesday that its president, Makoto Yamashina, intends to resign his post to become chairman to take responsibility for the failed merger.

Shares of the toymaker had strengthened in the months following the merger plan announcement, helped by booming sales of its "Tamagotchi" toy. Bandai shareholders were to receive 0.76 of a Sega share for each of their Bandai shares.

"There is disappointment among investors that the team-up of the two firms...failed but the Bandai gains prompted by the merger ratio are melting away, adding to the losses," said Harushige Kobayashi, deputy general manager of Yamaichi Securities.
"Sega, which was to be the surviving company, fell when the merger was first announced due to worries over an unclear future," he added.
But despite the weakness in Bandai's shares on Wednesday, analysts say that when the outlook for the two firms is compared, Bandai's future looks rosier.
Bandai's shares are likely to be weak for a while as there concern remains about discord within its management, said Yasuaki Fujine, an analyst at Smith Barney International Inc.
"But it will be able to benefit from Tamagotchi in the 1997/98 fiscal year," he said.
Hironobu Sawaki, an analyst at Nikko Research Center, said Sega could have acquired distribution routes for children's goods and Bandai's sales know-how through a merger.

"There was nothing formally decided about the merger as far as actual business was concerned and the merger never got off the ground, so there was nothing really lost," said Mitsuko Morita, an analyst at Morgan Stanley Japan.
Bandai and Sega said they would pursue a business tie-up in lieu of a merger.
